record.paper_title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science
record.original_question: Are biologically important precursor molecules actually produced in Titan's atmosphere, beyond the complex hydrocarbons and nitriles already detected, and can future spectroscopy and in situ chemical analysis determine the molecular composition and structure of large organic molecules relevant to prebiotic chemistry?

evidence.quote: 19) Are there important biological precursor molecules produced in the atmosphere?

The combination of the detected complex organic chemistry along with the laboratory simulations showing the potential for prebiotic molecules to arise has naturally led to the question of whether such prebiotic molecules also occur on Titan.

Despite some of Cassini’s instruments (especially CAPS) being able to detect the presence of large organic molecules, the instruments did not have the ability determine the molecular composition or structure.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Saturn's largest moon, Titan, possesses a dense nitrogen–methane atmosphere in which photochemistry and energetic-particle chemistry are known to produce a wide variety of complex hydrocarbons and nitriles (e.g., HCN, HC3N, C2H2, C6H6, and heavier tholin-like aerosols). Laboratory simulations of Titan-like atmospheres have demonstrated pathways yielding molecules of prebiotic interest, including amino acids and nucleobases, upon hydrolysis or further processing of tholins. Determine whether biologically relevant prebiotic precursor molecules — such as amino acids, nucleobases, sugars, or their immediate precursors — are actually formed in situ in Titan's atmosphere beyond the already-detected suite of hydrocarbons and nitriles. Specifically: (a) identify which classes of prebiotic precursor molecules can be produced by gas-phase and aerosol chemistry under realistic Titan atmospheric conditions (temperature, pressure, UV/EUV flux, magnetospheric and cosmic-ray inputs, methane and nitrogen mixing ratios), (b) predict their abundances, vertical distributions, and isomeric/structural forms, and (c) specify the spectroscopic signatures and in situ mass-spectrometric/chromatographic measurement strategies (with required mass resolution, sensitivity, and structural-discrimination capability) sufficient to determine the molecular composition and structure of large organic molecules in Titan's atmosphere and haze.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a recognized open question in Titan science. Cassini's instruments (notably CAPS and INMS) detected large organic ions and neutrals but lacked the mass resolution and structural-analysis capability to identify specific prebiotic molecules. The upcoming Dragonfly mission (planned launch 2028, arrival 2034) and proposed orbiter/spectroscopy missions are expected to address this question, but as of 2026 no in situ identification of prebiotic precursors in Titan's atmosphere has been achieved.

status_evidence.title: Dragonfly mission overview
status_evidence.snippet: Dragonfly is a NASA rotorcraft-lander mission to Titan to investigate prebiotic chemistry and habitability, scheduled for launch in 2028 and arrival in 2034.
status_evidence.claim: Identification of prebiotic molecules on Titan remains a target of future missions, indicating the question is currently open.

status_evidence.title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science (arXiv:2501.00971)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists detection of biological precursor molecules in Titan's atmosphere as an outstanding open question.
status_evidence.claim: Recent community review treats the question as open.
